2.title: Two Voices, One Choice

story.title: Neha and the Group Project
story.content:
The group project was due on Friday, and Neha's notebook had become a battlefield of its own.

On the left page she had written, in blue ink: "Tell the truth. Priya copied three paragraphs from Wikipedia. It is not fair to the rest of us who worked honestly." On the right page, in pencil so soft it was almost invisible: "Priya is your friend. She has been having trouble at home. If you report her, she might fail the whole term. Is that what a friend does?"

Neha stared at both columns until the words blurred.

The project was a history presentation on the Mauryan Empire — twenty slides, a spoken script, and a bibliography that had to be properly sourced. Neha, Rohan, and Priya had divided the work three weeks ago. Neha had done the research on Ashoka's edicts. Rohan had built the slide design. Priya was responsible for the opening section on Chandragupta.

Yesterday, when Neha opened their shared document to combine sections, she recognised three paragraphs in Priya's part word-for-word from a website she had used herself during research. Priya had not rewritten them. She had not cited them. She had pasted and changed the font colour, as if that made it invisible.

Neha's stomach tightened. She closed the laptop. Opened it. Closed it again.

At lunch, Priya sat across from her eating her paratha with unusual quietness. "Is everything okay with the project?" she asked, not quite meeting Neha's eyes.

"Fine," Neha said. It was not fine.

That evening, Neha's Appa found her at the dining table with both pages of the notebook open. He read them without speaking, then poured two glasses of water and sat down.

"Which voice is louder?" he asked.

"Both," Neha said miserably. "That's the problem."

Appa nodded. "In the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna faces something like this — not a group project, but the same feeling. He sees people he loves on the other side of the battlefield. He sees his duty as a warrior. Both feel true. Both feel impossible. He tells Krishna: I am confused about my duty. I am your disciple. Please instruct me clearly what I should do."

"What did Krishna say?"

"First, he did not mock the confusion. Arjuna's conflict was real — love and duty genuinely pulling against each other. Krishna treated that seriously. But he also did not let Arjuna stay frozen forever in the middle. He asked him to look clearly at both sides, speak honestly about what he saw, and then choose with wisdom rather than panic."

Neha was quiet for a long moment.

"I don't want to destroy Priya," she said.

"And you don't want to betray your own honesty," Appa said. "Those are both good values. The question is not which one wins. The question is: what action honours both as much as possible?"

The next morning, Neha asked Priya to meet her in the library before school. She did not accuse. She said: "I noticed some sections that look copied. I think we need to fix them together before we submit. Can we sit down today and rewrite them properly?"

Priya's face went red. Then she nodded, slowly. "I was overwhelmed," she whispered. "My parents have been fighting every night. I ran out of time."

"I know," Neha said. "That's why I didn't go straight to the teacher. But we still have to fix it."

They spent two hours rewriting. It was awkward and uncomfortable and, by the end, more honest than any easy silence would have been.

Emotional conflict had not vanished. But Neha had learned what Arjuna learned on the chariot: when two true things pull against each other, the answer is not to pretend one of them is false. The answer is to see clearly, speak honestly, and choose.

2.title: When Sorrow Runs Deep

story.title: Ishaan and Coach Meera
story.content:
Ishaan had not touched his cricket bat in two weeks.

It leaned against his bedroom wall like a stranger — the same bat he had scored forty-two runs with in the district semifinal, the bat whose handle he had rewound with fresh grip tape the night before the match that changed everything. He could not look at it without feeling something crack open inside his chest.

The match had been winnable. Ishaan's school needed eight runs off the last over with two wickets in hand. He had been at the crease, calm, counting the bowler's rhythm the way Coach Meera had taught him. Then on the fourth ball, a sharp catch at mid-wicket. Out. The next batsman run out. Done.

The team had lost by three runs.

Ishaan had walked off the field without speaking to anyone. He had not cried in front of his teammates — he waited until he was in the bathroom at home with the tap running. But the sorrow did not stay in that bathroom. It followed him to breakfast, to class, to bed. It sat on his chest like a stone.

"I can't do it again," he told his Amma on the Tuesday after. "What's the point? I had one job — eight runs — and I failed. Every time I think about cricket I feel sick."

Amma called Coach Meera.

Coach Meera arrived on Thursday afternoon with mangoes from her garden and no cricket gear. She sat on the floor of Ishaan's room — not on the chair he offered — and peeled a mango in silence until the sweet smell filled the room.

"Tell me the worst part," she said.

Ishaan stared at the bat on the wall. "I let everyone down. The whole team practiced for months. And I — I couldn't even score eight runs. I'd rather never play again than feel this again."

Coach Meera was quiet. Then she said: "Do you know what Arjuna told Krishna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, when his sorrow was so deep he could not fight?"

Ishaan shook his head.

"He said: I cannot kill my own teachers and family, even for a kingdom. What pleasure would victory bring? What use is a kingdom if the people I love are destroyed? I do not want to fight. I would rather be killed unarmed than kill them."

"That's — really sad," Ishaan said.

"It is. And Krishna did not say: stop being dramatic. He did not tell Arjuna his feelings were silly. Arjuna's sorrow was real and deep and it came from love — love for his teachers, his family, his whole world. Krishna heard all of it."

Coach Meera handed him a slice of mango. "But Krishna also did not leave Arjuna in that sorrow forever. He began to teach — gently at first, then more firmly. He helped Arjuna see that his pain was honest, but his conclusion — that doing nothing was better than doing his duty — needed to be examined."

"So my feelings are okay but giving up isn't?"

"Your feelings are real. They deserve to be felt. But feelings are not always the full truth. You are not only the boy who got caught at mid-wicket. You are also the boy who scored forty-two runs to get your team there. You are also the boy who has courage enough to pick up the bat again — not because the sorrow has gone, but because cricket is still part of who you are."

Ishaan took the mango. It was very sweet.

The next Saturday, he did not go to the full team practice. He asked Coach Meera to meet him at the nets alone. He picked up the bat. His hands shook a little. He played anyway.

Deep sorrow had not been dismissed. It had been met — with honesty, with patience, and with a path forward.

2.title: The Soul and the Seasons
2.micro_theme: The soul, change, and life's opposites

story.title: Ananya's Four-Season Journal
story.content:
Ananya started the journal because her science teacher, Ms. Pillai, assigned it — but by October it had become something she actually needed.

The assignment was simple: track one object in nature through four seasons. Most students chose a tree or a bird's nest. Ananya chose the neem tree in her grandmother's courtyard in Hyderabad, the one with bark rough enough to scrape her palms when she climbed it as a smaller child.

Summer entry, written in June: "The neem is loud with leaves. Crows argue in the branches every morning. I feel hot and happy and annoyed by my brother in equal amounts. Everything is bright."

Monsoon entry, August: "Rain hammers the leaves. The ground smells like wet earth and jasmine from Paati's garden. I feel cozy inside but restless — stuck indoors, missing my friends. Same tree, different mood."

Winter entry, January: "The neem looks stripped and honest. No pretending to be full. I feel quiet too. School exams are close. Some days I am confident. Some days I am sure I will fail everything."

Spring entry, March: "Tiny green shoots on branches that looked dead. I felt surprised by hope. Then I got into an argument with my best friend Meera and felt terrible again. Both things true on the same day."

When Ananya read all four entries aloud in class, Ms. Pillai nodded slowly. "Notice something? The tree changed. You changed. But it was always the same tree — and always you."

That evening, Ananya video-called Paati and showed her the journal. Paati adjusted her reading glasses and smiled. "Your Ms. Pillai is wise. Let me tell you what Krishna taught Arjuna about this."

Paati's voice grew gentle and steady. "Krishna said: never was there a time when you or I did not exist, nor will there be a time when we cease to be. The soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body — just as the body itself passes through seasons. Heat and cold, pleasure and pain — they come and go. They are like visitors at a door. The wise person does not let them disturb their inner steadiness."

Ananya flipped to a blank page. "So the soul is like — the tree underneath the seasons?"

"Something like that," Paati said. "The leaves fall. New leaves come. The tree looks completely different in winter and summer. But the neem is still the neem. Your feelings change — happy, sad, angry, hopeful — sometimes all in one day. That is natural. You are not broken because you feel opposites. You are human."

"But what stays the same?"

Paati thought for a moment. "Your capacity to grow. Your ability to learn. The love you carry for people — even when you are angry at them. The you that watches all the seasons pass."

Ananya drew a neem tree on the blank page with four panels — green, rain-grey, bare, budding. In the centre of the trunk she wrote one word: still here.

When she moved to a new city the following year and lost the courtyard and the tree and her old street, she brought the journal. On lonely evenings she opened it and remembered: everything outside changes. The soul that watches — that learns, that loves, that keeps going — travels through all of it.

2.title: What Cannot Be Destroyed

story.title: Rahul and the House That Moved
story.content:
Everything familiar disappeared in three weeks.

Rahul's family sold the yellow house on Tulip Lane — the one with the broken gate that squeaked, the guava tree he had climbed since he was five, the window seat where he read comics until Amma called him for dinner. Appa's company was transferring him to Pune. New flat, new school, new everything.

Rahul packed his room in silence. Each object he placed in a box felt like putting a piece of himself in storage. His cricket trophies. His bookshelf with the spine-cracked Harry Potters. The poster of the Mars rover he had taped above his desk and replaced three times because the corners kept peeling.

On the last night, he sat on the empty window seat and thought: if all of this goes, what is left of me?

The new flat in Pune was on the fourteenth floor. It had clean white walls and a view of other identical buildings. Rahul's new room was the right size but felt like a hotel — temporary, borrowed, not his. At the new school, he ate lunch alone for the first week. His old friends sent messages, but the messages made him miss home harder, so he stopped reading them.

His Chithappa — his uncle who lived in Pune — visited on a Sunday with filter coffee and a chess set.

"You look like someone who lost more than a house," Chithappa said, setting up the board on the small balcony table.

"I did," Rahul said. "I lost everything."

Chithappa moved a pawn. "Did you?"

"My room. My tree. My friends. My whole life."

"Those things changed. That is true. They hurt to lose — that is also true." Chithappa looked at him steadily. "But let me tell you what Krishna said to Arjuna when Arjuna was afraid that everything meaningful would be destroyed on the battlefield. Krishna said: there has never been a time when you did not exist, and there will never be a time when you cease to be. What is real in you — the Self — cannot be cut by weapons, burned by fire, soaked by water, or dried by wind. It is eternal, unchanging, ever-present."

Rahul frowned. "That sounds very — cosmic. I'm just a kid who moved schools."

Chithappa smiled. "Cosmic things come in small packages. Think practically. What did you bring with you that no moving truck carried?"

Rahul was quiet. "I still know how to climb a tree — even if there isn't one here yet. I still make people laugh when I want to. I still care about cricket and Mars and finishing a book even when the ending is sad."

"There," Chithappa said. "That caring, that curiosity, that Rahul-ness — the truck did not take it. The white walls did not erase it. New school cannot destroy it unless you decide it has."

They played chess until the sun went down. Rahul lost twice and won once.

The next week, he joined the school cricket trial. His hands were nervous. His batting was still his batting — a little rusty, but real. A boy named Dev watched him play and said, "You hit that ball like you mean it. Sit with us at lunch?"

The yellow house was gone. But the indestructible things — curiosity, courage, the ability to begin again — had made the journey too.

2.title: The Flame That Stayed
2.micro_theme: The body ends; the soul does not

story.title: Kavya and Thatha's Brass Diya
story.content:
Kavya was nine when Thatha died, old enough to understand the word "gone" and young enough to not fully believe it.

Thatha had been the person who walked her to the corner shop every Sunday for peppermints, who told her stories about Krishna and Arjuna on the chariot while she braided her Amma's old dupatta through his fingers, who lit a brass diya every evening in the small alcove near the front door where the smell of camphor and sandalwood lived permanently in the wood.

The funeral had been long and full of people speaking in low voices. Kavya wore a white kurta and held Amma's hand and did not cry until everyone left and the house went quiet. Then she cried until her throat hurt.

For weeks after, she avoided the alcove. The brass diya sat there untouched, a thin line of old wax frozen along the rim. Every time she passed it, her chest tightened. Thatha had lit it. Thatha was not here. Therefore the diya should not be lit. The logic felt airtight and unbearable.

Her Paati — Thatha's wife — noticed. One evening she found Kavya on the sofa with a book she was not reading.

"Come with me," Paati said.

She led Kavya to the alcove, picked up the brass diya, and polished it with her pallu until it gleamed. Then she looked at Kavya with eyes that were sad and clear at the same time.

"You are older now than when you first heard the story of the little lamp," Paati said. "You deserve the deeper version."

She lit the wick. The flame caught — small, orange, steady, alive.

"When Arjuna was broken with grief on the battlefield, Krishna did not only tell him to stand up. He taught him about the soul. He said: the soul is never born, and it never dies. It is not slain when the body is slain. The one who thinks the soul kills or is killed does not know the truth. The soul is eternal."

Kavya watched the flame. "Thatha's body died," she said quietly. "I saw the coffin."

"Yes," Paati said. "And that is real, and your grief is real, and I will never tell you to pretend otherwise. Bodies begin and end. Bodies get old and sick and stop. That is the way of all living things — the diya's wax, the wick, the holder. They wear out."

"So Thatha is just — gone?"

Paati shook her head. "The body is gone. The person you loved — his stories, his kindness, the way he made you feel safe, the love he gave you — where does love go when someone dies?"

Kavya thought about it. "It stays," she whispered. "It stays in me."

"And in me," Paati said, placing Kavya's palm over her own heart, then over Paati's. "And in every person he touched. The soul is like the flame — you can snuff the wick, but the light does not vanish from the universe. It joins what is already bright."

Kavya looked at the diya. "Will you teach me to light it?"

Paati nodded. "Every evening. The way he did. Not because he is sitting here — but because the love he lit in you is still burning."

That night, Kavya's hands shook a little as she held the match. The flame rose. She was still sad — grief did not disappear like switching off a light. But the fear that Thatha had been completely erased began to soften.

The body ends. The love — the soul's light — does not.

story.title: Vikram's Science Fair Discovery
story.content:
Vikram's science fair project was about change — and it changed something in him too.

He had chosen a topic his teacher called "ambitious": demonstrating how matter transforms but never truly disappears. His display board had three sections. Section one: a piece of paper burned in a metal tray — ash left behind, but the matter had gone somewhere, into smoke and heat. Section two: an ice cube melted in a beaker — solid to liquid, same water, different form. Section three: his Appa's old cotton shirt cut into strips and rewoven on a small loom Paati had in her cupboard — new shape, same threads.

The morning of the fair, Vikram stood beside his board nervously adjusting the strips of rewoven cloth. A judge in a blue lanyard stopped and read his title: "Changing Forms, Continuing Essence."

"Explain this to me," the judge said.

Vikram took a breath. "Fire can burn paper, but the stuff the paper was made of doesn't vanish — it changes form. Water can melt ice, freeze it again, boil it into steam. The water is still water. And cloth — " he held up the rewoven strip, " — can be cut and woven into something new, but the cotton fibres are the same fibres."

The judge nodded. "And the Gita connection? Your teacher mentioned you had one."

Vikram had not expected this question in front of other students. He felt his ears go warm. But he had practiced with Appa, so he answered:

"In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna teaches Arjuna that the soul is like this. Weapons cannot cut it. Fire cannot burn it. Water cannot wet it. Wind cannot dry it. When the body dies, the soul does not die — it passes into a new body the way a person changes worn clothes for new ones. The clothes change. The person wearing them does not."

The judge looked genuinely interested. "And what does that mean for you — not cosmically, but practically?"

Vikram thought about his grandmother, who had died the previous year. He thought about the caterpillar enclosure in Class 4, where they had watched chrysalises split open and butterflies emerge — same creature, utterly different body. He thought about himself — how much he had changed since he was six, and yet he was still somehow the same Vikram who loved science and hated coriander.

"It means — " he said slowly, " — bodies and situations change, but the important part of a person doesn't get destroyed by change. My Ajji died, but what she taught me is still here." He touched his chest. "I changed schools last year and I was terrified. But I was still me underneath. The soul — the real me — keeps going through all of it."

He did not win first prize. He won the "Curiosity and Connection" award, which came with a book voucher and a handshake that made him stand taller.

That evening, Appa found him re-reading the Gita passage he had quoted — the one about weapons, fire, water, and wind. "Accurate science and accurate scripture," Appa said, amused.

"Same idea," Vikram said. "Different words."

He pinned the rewoven cloth strip above his desk as a reminder: forms change. Essence continues.

2.title: Do Your Duty, Release the Grip
2.micro_theme: Duty without fear of wrong result

story.title: Sanjay and the District Debate
story.content:
Sanjay had rehearsed his debate speech forty-seven times.

He knew this because his Appa had suggested he keep tally marks on the back of his cue cards — not to make him anxious, Appa said, but so he could see how much honest work he had done when fear tried to convince him otherwise. Forty-seven tallies. Three weeks of research on whether schools should ban smartphones in classrooms. Arguments for: focus, sleep, face-to-face friendship. Arguments against: safety, learning tools, trust.

Sanjay believed in his position — limited phone use during school hours, with exceptions for emergencies. He had built a careful case. He had timed his speech to exactly four minutes and fifty seconds.

But on the morning of the district debate, fear arrived anyway.

It showed up as a voice in his head while he ate his idli: "What if you forget your opening line? What if the judge asks something you can't answer? What if you embarrass yourself in front of the whole auditorium? What if you lose and everyone thinks you're not smart?"

Sanjay's hands went cold around his water bottle.

His coach, Ms. Rekha, found him in the warm-up room pacing in a tight line. "You're doing the walk," she said. "That's the fear walk. Sit down."

He sat.

"I'm prepared," he said. "I know I'm prepared. But I keep thinking about what happens if I fail."

Ms. Rekha pulled a folded paper from her bag — a printed verse she kept for debate days. "Read the underlined part," she said.

Sanjay read: "Considering your duty as a warrior, you should not waver. For a warrior, there is no greater good than fighting a righteous battle. Even if you lose, fighting with honour is itself the victory."

"That's from the Gita," Sanjay said. "Arjuna on the battlefield."

"Yes. And Krishna's deeper point — which comes a little later — is this: you have a right to your action, but you do not have a right to the fruits of action. Do not be attached to outcomes. Do not be attached to avoiding outcomes. Do your duty with your best effort and let the result come as it comes."

Sanjay stared at the card. "So I should not care if I win?"

"Care about doing your best. Care about speaking truthfully. Care about representing your school with integrity. But release your grip on the trophy — because gripping it too hard is what makes your hands cold right now."

Sanjay breathed out slowly. He thought about all forty-seven tallies. The work was done. The speech was ready. What happened after he walked on stage was not entirely in his hands — the judge's mood, the other speaker's skill, a moment of forgetfulness he could not predict.

What was in his hands was the next four minutes and fifty seconds.

He walked onto the stage. The auditorium was larger than he expected — rows of faces, a timer on the screen, the other school's speaker already seated, looking calm. Sanjay's heart hammered. He placed his cue cards on the podium, found the first line, and began.

He stumbled once — a half-second pause where a word escaped him — and then recovered. He spoke clearly. He answered the cross-question without panic. When the results were announced, he placed second.

Not first. Second.

In the corridor afterward, Appa hugged him one-armed, careful of the cue cards. "How do you feel?"

Sanjay thought about it honestly. "Disappointed," he said. "But also — okay. I did the work. I showed up. I didn't run away."

"That," Appa said, "is the victory Krishna was talking about."

Duty done without fear of the wrong result. That was enough for today.

2.title: One Arrow, One Target

story.title: Meera's Scattered Evening
story.content:
Meera had been "studying" for forty minutes and had accomplished almost nothing.

Her textbook was open to page forty-two — the chapter on photosynthesis — but her eyes had not moved past the first paragraph in twenty minutes. Her phone buzzed on the desk: a message from her friend group about weekend plans. She picked it up, replied with three emojis, then opened a short video "just for a minute." The minute became twelve. She remembered the textbook, switched back, read two sentences, and then noticed her pencil case was messy and spent six minutes reorganising it by colour.

When Amma called from the kitchen — "Meera, how is study going?" — she said "Fine!" without hesitation. It was not fine. Her mind felt like a room with twenty doors, all of them open, wind blowing through from every direction.

The science test was on Thursday. It was Monday evening.

On Tuesday, Meera's science teacher Mr. Das wrote a quote on the board during class: "Many-branched and endless are the thoughts of the irresolute. For the resolute in purpose, there is but one thought." He asked if anyone knew where it came from.

Meera raised her hand before she could overthink it. "The Bhagavad Gita," she said. "Krishna teaching Arjuna about focused intelligence."

Mr. Das smiled. "Correct. Krishna tells Arjuna that a person whose mind scatters in many directions has no steady goal. But a person who gathers their intelligence like an archer drawing a bow — one target, one arrow, one clear aim — that person finds the path."

After class, Meera stayed back. "Sir, my mind is the scattered one. I sit down to study and end up everywhere except the textbook."

Mr. Das did not lecture her. He pulled out a blank index card. "Write the one thing you need to finish in the next thirty minutes. Just one. Not the whole chapter — one section, one page, one concept."

Meera wrote: Read page 42–43 and summarise photosynthesis in five sentences.

"Now," Mr. Das said, "phone in your bag, not on the desk. Timer for thirty minutes. Until the timer rings, those five sentences are your only target. One arrow. One aim."

That evening, Meera tried it at her desk. She put her phone inside her school bag and zipped it closed. She set a timer on her watch — not her phone — for thirty minutes. She read page forty-two. She read page forty-three. She wrote five sentences, the last one slightly smudged because her hand was tired, but complete.

The timer rang. She had done one thing.

She took a five-minute break — standing up, stretching, drinking water — and then wrote a new card: Draw and label the photosynthesis diagram on page forty-four.

One target. One arrow.

By Wednesday evening, she had worked through the whole chapter in small, focused blocks rather than one chaotic hour of scattered attention. Her mind still wandered sometimes — she was human, not a machine — but each time it wandered, she looked at the card on her desk and asked: what is the one target right now?

On Thursday, she walked into the science test with steady hands. Not because she knew every answer — she did not — but because her preparation had been focused rather than frantic.

Krishna's teaching was not about never getting distracted. It was about gathering the scattered mind back to one clear aim, again and again, like an archer returning to the bow.

story.title: Kavya's Study Storm
story.content:
Kavya had turned her study desk into a battlefield between two kings: Panic and Perfection.

Two weeks before her Class 8 annual exams, she had read online that top students study fourteen hours a day. So she tried. She stacked textbooks from floor to ceiling, set three alarms, and promised herself she would not leave her chair until midnight. By day three her head ached like someone had tied a rubber band around it. She forgot which chapter she was on. She cried into her maths notebook and told her mother, 'I am useless.'

The next morning, ashamed of the crying, Kavya swung to the other extreme. She left her books closed on the desk and told herself exams did not matter anyway. She watched two episodes of her favourite show, then three. She scrolled through reels until her thumb felt sore. She ate biscuits for lunch and avoided the dining table where Amma had saved hot dal and rice. By evening, guilt sat in her stomach heavier than the biscuits. 'Tomorrow I will study properly,' she promised. Tomorrow she panicked again and studied too hard until midnight. The cycle repeated.

Her Sanskrit teacher, Sri Venkatesh sir, noticed Kavya zoning out during a revision class. After the bell, he asked her to stay. He did not scold her. He opened his own copy of the Bhagavad Gita on the staff table, worn soft at the corners.

'There is a teaching Krishna gives Arjuna in Chapter Two,' he said. 'Arjuna is caught between grief on the battlefield and the demand to act. Krishna tells him to rise above the three modes — the push toward frantic doing, the pull toward giving up, and the foggy middle where we just drift. Transcend the extremes, Krishna says. Be rooted in wisdom. Then perform your duty without being a slave to panic or laziness.'

Kavya frowned. 'But I still have to study, sir.'

'Exactly. Duty remains. Only the wild swinging stops. You are not a machine that must run fourteen hours. You are not a stone that must ignore exams. You are a student. Your duty is honest preparation — steady blocks, food, sleep, one chapter at a time.'

Together they wrote a simple timetable on the back of her rough notebook: ninety minutes of focused study, a fifteen-minute walk on the terrace, another ninety minutes, then dinner and lights out by ten. No fourteen-hour marathons. No biscuit-only afternoons.

The first evening felt almost suspiciously calm. Kavya opened her science chapter on respiration and read four pages without checking her phone. She paused when her eyes grew tired instead of pushing through in a fog. The next morning she ate proper breakfast before revising algebra.

On exam day, Kavya did not feel like a superhero. She felt prepared enough. Her hands were steady when she read the first question. The extremes had not disappeared from the world — she still saw classmates boasting about all-nighters — but she had stopped obeying them.

Krishna's lesson is not to escape life's duties. It is to rise above the all-or-nothing storm inside, then do what is yours to do with quiet steadiness.
story.content_te:
కావ్య తన చదువు బల్లను రెండు రాజుల మధ్య యుద్ధభూమిగా మార్చింది: పానిక్ మరియు పరిపూర్ణత.

ఎనిమిదవ తరగతి వార్షిక పరీక్షలకు రెండు వారాల ముందు, టాప్ విద్యార్థులు రోజుకు పద్నాలుగు గంటలు చదువుతారని ఆన్‌లైన్‌లో చదివింది. అదే ప్రయత్నించింది. పాఠ్యపుస్తకాలను నేల నుండి పైకి పేర్చింది, మూడు అలారాలు పెట్టింది, అర్ధరాత్రి వరకు కుర్చీలోనే ఉంటానని నిర్ణయించుకుంది. మూడవ రోజు తల నొప్పి — ఎవరో రబ్బర్ బ్యాండ్ కట్టినట్లు. ఏ అధ్యాయం చదువుతున్నాదో మర్చిపోయింది. గణిత నోట్‌బుక్‌లో ఏడ్చింది, అమ్మకు 'నేను పనికిరాని' అని చెప్పింది.

తర్వాత ఉదయం, ఏడ్చినందుకు సిగ్గుపడి, కావ్య మరొక అతివ్యయం వైపు తిరిగింది. పుస్తకాలు మూసి ఉంచి పరీక్షలు ఏమీ ముఖ్యం కావు అని తనకు తాను చెప్పుకుంది. ఇష్టమైన షో రెండు ఎపిసోడ్లు, తర్వాత మూడు. రీల్స్ స్క్రోల్ చేసి బొటనవేలు నొప్పి. భోజనానికి బిస్కెట్లు, అమ్మ వేడి అన్నం పెట్టిన డైనింగ్ టేబుల్‌కు వెళ్ళలేదు. సాయంత్రం అపరాధభావం బిస్కెట్ల కంటే ఎక్కువ బరువుగా. 'రేపు సరిగ్గా చదువుతాను' — రేపు మళ్ళీ పానిక్, అర్ధరాత్రి వరకు చదువు. ఈ చక్రం పునరావృతమైంది.

సంస్కృత ఉపాధ్యాయుడు శ్రీ వెంకటేశ్ సర్ పునరావృత్త తరగతిలో కావ్య మనసు తప్పిపోవడం గమనించారు. గంట మోగిన తర్వాత ఆమెను ఆపాడు. తిట్టలేదు. స్టాఫ్ టేబుల్ మీద తన భగవద్గీతా కాపీ తెరిచాడు — మూలలు మృదువుగా అరిగి ఉన్నాయి.

'అధ్యాయం రెండులో కృష్ణుడు అర్జునునికి ఇచ్చే బోధ ఉంది' అన్నారు. 'యుద్ధభూమిలో దుఃఖం మరియు చర్య అవసరం మధ్య అర్జునుడు చిక్కుకున్నాడు. కృష్ణుడు మూడు గుణాల పైకి ఎగరమన్నాడు — అతి చేయడం, వదిలివేయడం, మరియు మధ్యలో తేలియాడే మబ్బు. అతివ్యయాలను అతిక్రమించు, జ్ఞానంలో నాటుకుని, పానిక్ లేదా సోమరితనానికి దాసుడిగా ఉండకుండా నీ బాధ్యత నిర్వహించు.'

కావ్య ముఖం ముడుచుకుంది. 'కానీ నేను ఇంకా చదవాలి సార్.'

'ఖచ్చితంగా. బాధ్యత మిగిలిపోతుంది. కేవలం ఊగే కదలిక ఆగుతుంది. నువ్వు పద్నాలుగు గంటలు పరిగెత్తే యంత్రం కాదు. పరీక్షలను పట్టించుకోని రాయి కాదు. నువ్వు విద్యార్థిని. నీ బాధ్యత నిజాయితీగల సన్నాహం — స్థిరమైన బ్లాకులు, ఆహారం, నిద్ర, ఒక్కో అధ్యాయం.'

కలిసి రఫ్ నోట్‌బుక్ వెనుక టైమ్‌టేబుల్ రాశారు: తొంభై నిమిషాలు ఫోకస్ చదువు, పదిహేను నిమిషాలు టెర్రస్ నడక, మరొక తొంభై నిమిషాలు, రాత్రి పదికి భోజనం మరియు నిద్ర. పద్నాలుగు గంటల మ్యారథాన్లు లేవు. బిస్కెట్ మాత్రమే ఉదయాలు లేవు.

మొదటి సాయంత్రం అనుమానంగా ప్రశాంతంగా అనిపించింది. శ్వాసక్రియ అధ్యాయం తెరిచి ఫోన్ చూడకుండా నాలుగు పేజీలు చదివింది. కళ్ళు అలసిపోతే మబ్బులో ముందుకు పోకుండా విరామం. తదుపరి ఉదయం భోజనం చేసి బీజగణితం పునరావృత్తం.

పరీక్ష రోజు కావ్య సూపర్‌హీరో లా అనిపించలేదు. సరిపడా సిద్ధంగా అనిపించింది. మొదటి ప్రశ్న చదివేటప్పుడు చేతులు స్థిరంగా ఉన్నాయి. ప్రపంచంలో అతివ్యయాలు అదృశ్యం కాలేదు — సహపాఠులు రాత్రంతా చదివామని గర్వపడటం చూసింది — కానీ వాటికి విధేయురాలు కాదు.

కృష్ణుని పాఠం జీవిత బాధ్యతల నుండి తప్పించుకోవడం కాదు. లోపల అన్నీ-లేదా-ఏమీ తుఫాను పైకి ఎగరి, నీది అయిన పనిని నిశ్శబ్ద స్థిరత్వంతో చేయడం.
story.moral: Rising above extremes does not mean avoiding your duty. It means stopping the swing between panic and giving up, then doing your work with steady, honest effort.
story.moral_te: అతివ్యయాల పైకి ఎగరడం అంటే బాధ్యత తప్పించుకోవడం కాదు. పానిక్ మరియు వదిలివేత మధ్య ఊగే కదలిక ఆపి, స్థిరమైన నిజాయితీ ప్రయత్నంతో పని చేయడం.

2.activity: Notice one area where you swing between 'all' and 'nothing.' Write a middle-path plan: one steady block of effort, one break, one rest time.
